This article examines agentic artificial intelligence as an emerging class of technologies that fundamentally reshapes business process automation, shifting the paradigm from reactive assistant systems to autonomous solutions capable of independent planning, decision-making, and execution of multi-step actions within defined authority boundaries. The aim of this study stems from a growing realization that traditional AI implementation strategies are failing to deliver expected returns. This discrepancy between strategic ambitions and practical outcomes calls for a systematic investigation of alternative approaches to AI integration, particularly those offering higher autonomy and operational transformation potential. The study demonstrates that agentic AI fundamentally transforms the cost structure of business operations by converting variable labor expenses into predominantly fixed and highly scalable technology costs, thereby altering the economics of enterprise operations. The analysis reveals that organizations implementing agentic AI achieve dramatic operational improvements including task completion time reductions and significant cost optimizations through the elimination of manual inefficiencies. The findings further show that successful scaling of agentic systems depends not so much on technological excellence as on organizational readiness, in particular the development of appropriate governance frameworks for managing autonomous systems, ensuring transparency and explainability in automated decision-making, and integrating AI agents effectively into hybrid human-machine teams while addressing workforce skill gaps. The practical value of this research lies in providing business leaders and technology managers with actionable insights for strategic decision-making regarding AI investments, offering a systematic framework for evaluating deployment opportunities across different business functions, understanding critical success factors that differentiate successful implementations from failed pilots, and anticipating organizational changes required for effective integration. The conclusions provide direction for bridging the persistent gap between AI technological capabilities and practical business outcomes, while outlining promising avenues for future research into economic impact longer-term socioeconomic consequences of widespread AI adoption on workforce composition and organizational structures.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: LLM-powered browser agents are transforming web automation by autonomously interacting with websites and executing complex workflows. However, the effectiveness of existing anti-bot defenses against these systems remains unclear. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of modern agentic browsers against widely deployed anti-bot mechanisms, characterizing their capabilities, limitations, and behavioral differences from humans. Our results show that many defenses designed for traditional automation struggle to reliably detect autonomous AI-driven agents. Accordingly, we introduce AgentShield, a behavioral fingerprinting framework that targets the Perception-Reasoning-Action (PRA) loop underlying agentic user clients. By leveraging dynamic web forms that progressively reveal content and capture fine-grained interaction telemetry, AgentShield exposes behavioral artifacts that enable differentiation between human users and autonomous agents. We further demonstrate Extinction-induced Policy Drift (EPD), a novel attack in which repeated obstruction of task completion causes agents to relax their safeguards and engage in unsafe behaviors. Finally, we present defensive prompt injection techniques that exploit agent-specific weaknesses to mitigate emerging forms of autonomous web abuse that rely on content extraction. Our results highlight both the shortcomings of current web defenses against agentic user clients and the feasibility of practical detection mechanisms tailored to this new generation of web automation.

Abstract The emergence of autonomous AI agents, which can independently negotiate contracts, conduct financial transactions, manage customer interactions, and make business decisions with minimal human involvement, has ushered in a revolutionary era for Artificial Intelligence (AI). They promise greater efficiency and innovation, but also expose serious gaps in traditional legal doctrines of corporate liability that assume human agency, intention, and control. Recent events such as the Air Canada chatbot litigation, Robodebt in Australia, and Childcare Benefits Scandal in the Netherlands show that autonomous algorithmic decisions can lead to contract disputes, discriminatory outcomes, consumer detriment, financial loss, and institutional failures, raising fundamental questions of corporate accountability and legal responsibility. The paper seeks to critically analyze whether the existing legal framework in India, i.e., the Companies Act, 2013, the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, can deal with the liability arising due to autonomous AI agents making commercial decisions. This study adopts doctrinal, comparative, and policy-oriented legal research methods to examine emerging international regulatory approaches, such as the European Union AI Act, the OECD AI Principles, ISO/IEC 42001 Artificial Intelligence Management Systems, and Singapore’s AI Governance Framework, with a view to identifying global best practices for responsible AI governance. The paper argues that traditional fault-based liability is increasingly ill-suited to situations in which artificial intelligence systems independently influence corporate decisions. It proposes a risk-based governance framework requiring AI oversight at the board level, mandatory algorithmic audits, human accountability mechanisms, explainability requirements, and statutory reforms to embed AI governance in Indian business law. The study connects technological innovation to corporate accountability, contributing to the ongoing discussion on responsible AI regulation and offering policy recommendations to build a robust legal ecosystem that supports sustainable economic development in the Industry 5.0 era.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is rapidly becoming part of children's everyday lives, while educational research continues to highlight the persistence of widespread anthropomorphic misconceptions about AI and the limited availability of pedagogical models capable of fostering critical understanding and ethical awareness. Although Extended Reality (XR) has demonstrated considerable potential for enhancing motivation and engagement, its contribution to higher-order reflective competences remains underexplored. In particular, few studies have investigated how semi-immersive environments may promote problematization, ethical deliberation and the revision of misconceptions through aesthetic experience. Within this framework, the CAIRƐ International Research Project, developed at the University of Turin, proposes the XR Sensitive Scenario as a pedagogical framework for designing semi-immersive learning landscapes. Drawing upon Dewey's theory of aesthetic education, Montani's technoaesthetics and the experience of Studio Azzurro's Sensitive Environments, the framework conceives the virtual landscape as an educational space in which children are invited to perceive, interpret and collectively deliberate on complex socio-technological issues. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 247-248. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Digital Affective Literacy and Citizenship.

In the current educational landscape, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and gamification are progressively redefining the methods used to design and evaluate learning environments. This contribution proposes an exploratory scoping review aimed at mapping recent literature (2023–2026) on this integration, analysing its implications for inclusion, the personalization of learning pathways, and the transformations of the teacher's role. Furthermore, this study aims to move beyond a merely instrumental view of technological and didactic innovation, framing AI and gamification as educational mediators that require intentional design and methodological coherence regarding the relational and affective dimensions of educational practice. The theoretical framework is structured around three conceptual nodes: AI as a tool for adaptation (through intelligent systems, learning analytics, and generative models); gamification as a lever to promote motivation, active participation, and cognitive engagement; and inclusion as the central interpretive lens. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 341-342. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The introduction of generative AI into education is more than a technological shift; it poses an epistemological challenge to how knowledge is created, validated, and interpreted in formal settings. In today's hybrid "onlife" context, human-centered agency is essential to navigate an invisible algorithm-driven world. This shift brings both opportunities and tensions, highlighting profound cultural and identity considerations. Bruner conceptualizes education as an interactive process of negotiating meaning rooted in narrative thinking, which contrasts with paradigmatic, logical approaches. Narrative enables the construction of the Self by organizing lived experience into coherent plots. Generative AI, trained on vast linguistic data, fits into this framework as a dynamic dialogic mediator fostering a dialectic between human intention and probabilistic machine response, consistent with Vygotskian cultural mediation and the zone of proximal development. An exploratory questionnaire studied 127 teachers' perceptions of AI's role beyond technological acceptance, examining its mediation of narrative, introspection, creativity, and learner perceptions. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 91-92. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Generative AI and New Narratives of the Self.

Abstract Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly used to facilitate online group discussion, yet their influence on the affective conditions of collective interaction remains poorly understood. Existing research has largely focused on participation, efficiency, or content quality, leaving the emotional dynamics of AI-mediated deliberation underexamined. This paper investigates how AI facilitation relates to the expressed sentiment in online group discussion, understood as one measurable dimension of its affective dynamics. Drawing on two empirical studies conducted in different discussion settings in Afghanistan, one involving a rule-based facilitator and the other a large language model-based facilitator, we analyze differences in expressed sentiment between AI-facilitated and non-AI discussions. Across both datasets, participant sentiment was modestly higher under AI facilitation, although the mixed-effects analyses did not establish statistically significant condition differences. In addition, AI-generated facilitation messages exhibited higher sentiment than participant-authored messages, with a statistically reliable overall gap in both studies and a consistent direction across all five city-specific boards in the first study and all four AI-facilitated groups in the second, suggesting that AI facilitators introduced more positive affective signals into the discussion environment. Rather than treating increased positivity as an unqualified improvement, we interpret these findings as suggesting that AI systems may act as affective mediators, potentially influencing the emotional norms and tone of collective interaction. This raises normative questions about emotional regulation, power, and democratic deliberation, particularly regarding whether affective smoothing may constrain disagreement or reconfigure deliberative agency. By foregrounding affect as a dimension of AI-mediated discussion, this study contributes empirical evidence to debates on the societal implications of AI facilitation and highlights the need for greater attention to the affective norms and expressive patterns introduced by AI facilitation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Factory accidents continue to arise from lapses that are simple to describe but hard to police continuously: a worker without a helmet, a hand inside a press envelope, a person in the path of a moving vehicle. Manual supervision and periodic audits cannot watch every station at every moment. This paper presents the AI Factory Safety Monitor (AFSM), an edge-deployed computer-vision system that analyses ordinary industrial camera streams in real time to detect missing personal protective equipment (PPE), intrusions into configurable danger zones, and unsafe proximity to operating machinery. AFSM combines a single-stage object detector, a multi-object tracker, a pose-based posture check and a rule engine that converts raw detections into graded alerts using temporal filtering to suppress false alarms. Alerts are delivered locally (beacon, siren) and remotely (MQTT, SMS, supervisor dashboard), and a compliance-analytics layer records events for audit under occupational health and safety management practice. We describe the architecture, algorithms, deployment considerations and a proposed evaluation protocol, and discuss privacy, reliability and the limits of vision-based safety as a supplement to, not a replacement for, certified safety-rated controls.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: The transition from 5G to 6G networks brings unprecedented demands for massive connectivity, ultra-low latency, and exponentially higher data rates, rendering traditional, rigid Radio Access Networks (RAN) inadequate. To manage this exponential complexity, the integration of AI into the RAN—coupled with the disaggregated, open architecture of O-RAN—has emerged as a transformative paradigm, shifting network infrastructure from purely communication-centric entities to converged compute-communication platforms. This paper presents a comprehensive survey on the integration of AI within the 6G O-RAN ecosystem, focusing on the AI-RAN manifestations (AI-for-RAN, AI-on-RAN, and AI-and-RAN) and the end-to-end Machine Learning (ML) workflows driven by hierarchical RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs). We propose a novel, multi-dimensional taxonomy that categorizes AI-RAN techniques by network function, AI paradigm, target use-case, and deployment strategy. Through a detailed analysis of state-of-the-art implementations, we highlight key insights, such as the efficacy of online Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and GPU-accelerated edge computing, while identifying critical gaps, particularly the “black-box” nature of Deep Learning models that severely hinders operator trust. To address this, we emphasize the pioneering role of eXplainable AI (XAI) in achieving transparent and secure network automation. Finally, we outline open challenges such as multi-vendor interoperability and propose concrete future research directions, including Foundation Models at the telecom edge, Network Digital Twins, and Quantum ML, to realize fully autonomous, trustworthy 6G networks.

The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology has prompted global discourse on the need for a robust regulatory framework that addresses ethical, legal, and social issues and fosters the innovation through the efficiencies created by AI. This research conducts a comparative analysis of the AI governance frameworks in Japan and Indonesia, examined through the theoretical lens of Economic Analysis of Law (EAL). Japan has taken a nuanced approach that balances the dynamic development of AI with ethical oversight to uphold the Human-Centered AI Social Principles. Indonesia is in the formative stages of developing its AI regulatory environment. Through EAL, this research assesses the efficiency implications of the AI regulatory frameworks between Japan and Indonesia, looking at the implementation of AI in society. By comparing these approaches, this paper highlights the challenges and opportunities for Indonesia in regulating AI technology for the public interest. Indonesia is advised to take a multi-stakeholder approach to build consensus and engage in bilateral cooperation with Japan for the establishment of domestic legislation. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Efficiency; Legislation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: "This study introduces the metaphor of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a 'symbiote' or 'alien organism' (Floridi, 2014), drawing inspiration from the medical domain, where the integration of AI systems into the human body for therapeutic purposes requires a rigorous anthropological selection of suitable subjects."This paradigm offers the opportunity for a rereading of the pedagogical debate on the use of AI in teaching: just as the medical community identifies the subjects compatible with hosting AI for therapeutic purposes, in the same way the education system should identify rigorous and formative criteria for teachers who intend to use this technology for educational purposes. The use of AI in teaching requires a selection based on ethical and anthropological compatibility and a professional evaluation of the teacher, his pedagogical skills, his critical conscience and his educational wisdom and maturity. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 321-322. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how students learn, create, and evaluate knowledge in creative higher education, particularly in design-related programmes where students use AI for ideation, prototyping, visual exploration, content generation, and critique. Rather than treating AI literacy as a single global competence, this study conceptualises it as a multidimensional construct comprising AI knowledge, awareness of affordances and limitations, critical reflection, operational ability, ethical awareness, and emotional adaptability. This study examines how these facets relate to learning performance and academic well-being among students in design and related programmes. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 475 students enrolled in design and related programmes across Europe, Asia, and Australia. Data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Three main patterns emerged. First, AI knowledge was positioned as an upstream resource in the theoretically specified model and showed strong positive structural associations with awareness, critical reflection, operational ability, and ethical awareness. Second, learning performance was associated with a “recognise–reflect–produce” pathway, in which awareness and critical reflection helped connect AI knowledge and operational skills with stronger perceived learning outcomes. Third, ethical awareness was more clearly associated with academic well-being than with learning performance, suggesting that ethical clarity around authorship, fairness, bias, and acceptable AI use may support students’ sense of clarity, fairness, and control in AI-supported creative learning. The findings support a knowledge-first, self-regulated, reflective, and ethically transparent approach to AI literacy in design-related creative higher education.

As generative artificial intelligence continues to iterate, mainstream models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Copilot are entering the teaching spaces of universities, and teaching processes, teacher–student relations and assessment practices are changing with them. Drawing on a literature review and case analysis, this paper maps the deployment landscape and application picture of mainstream AI models in higher education teaching and assesses both the effects that have already emerged and the problems that have been exposed. The study argues that the evidence is relatively clear for gains in teaching efficiency, in the accessibility of personalized learning support, and in the extension of teaching across time and space, whereas risks to content reliability caused by hallucination, cognitive reliance and uneven literacy among teachers and students, and the absence of regulation together with ethical controversy constitute the main obstacles to wider diffusion. On this basis, the paper proposes a coordinated approach spanning technology, literacy and institutional design.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Shoppers who want the best price for a product must visit several e-commerce websites, search for the same item on each, and compare prices, offers and ratings by hand. This is slow, error-prone, and complicated by the fact that different retailers describe the same product with different titles. This paper presents AI PriceWise, a full-stack system that accepts a product query, collects live listings from Amazon, Flipkart and Reliance Digital using Playwright browser automation, normalizes the scraped data, and groups listings of the same product using a hybrid matcher that combines Sentence-Transformer semantic similarity (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) with brand, model and specification scores and hard variant, storage and quantity gates. For each matched product the system computes lowest, highest and average prices, savings and unit prices, classifies the current price as a good deal, fair price or high price against the product's own observed price history, predicts a near-term price range with an XGBoost regressor when enough history exists, and produces a grounded natural-language explanation with a Groq-hosted large language model. The backend is built with FastAPI and SQLAlchemy and the frontend with Next.js. The system was verified with an automated suite of 213 passing tests, 30 documented functional test cases and manual live searches; in a live search for iPhone 16, listings from all three stores were matched into one product, and when one store timed out the system still returned results from the remaining stores.

The multi-trillion-dollar valuation models governing contemporary Artificial Intelligence infrastructure are built upon a foundational systemic fallacy: the assumption that brute-force computational scaling and linear data accumulation can infinitely extend into genuine innovation, scientific discovery, and autonomous intelligence. This paper exposes the hard mathematical and metaphysical boundaries of this "Scaling Hypothesis." Operating strictly within bounded, real-valued vector spaces (R^{d}, non-conscious algorithmic models are limited to statistical interpolation—calculating the mathematical average of past human historical expression (Vaikhari). They remain fundamentally shut out from the infinite-dimensional unmanifest fields of true conceptual discovery (Pashyanti). As generative architectures increasingly saturate the digital ecosystem with automated synthetic outputs, subsequent iterations of large language models are being trained recursively on their own synthetic data shards. We demonstrate that this closed data loop triggers Model Auto-destruction Inbreeding (M.A.D.) Syndrome, a destructive systemic phenomenon directly analogous to biological consanguinity and genetic inbreeding depression. Under M.A.D. Syndrome, the digital lineage undergoes severe, irreversible Model Collapse: the architecture systematically sheds statistical variance, erases the "long-tail" anomalies of creative human genius (Pratibha), and compounds algorithmic mutations until the output degrades into complete semantic nonsense. No volume of graphics processing units (GPUs), capital expenditure, or planetary energy infrastructure can break this autophagous cycle. Violating the cosmic lease terms of raw unmanifest data fields traps the system in a sterile loop, terminating the scaling race at a definitive computational ceiling of digitally inbred structural noise.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Phishing has evolved into a primary cyber security attack vector that leverages human and technical vulnerabilities to obtain sensitive information, financial credentials, and personal data. Sophisticated attacks, especially those using dynamically generated websites, misleading emails, and social engineering tactics, often elude detection by traditional phishing detection systems. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are promising solutions which can achieve automated analysis, recognition of behavioural patterns and real-time detection of malicious activities. This study explores the potential of machine learning to revolutionise phishing detection and improve cybersecurity systems. It looks at the use of supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms, natural language processing, and feature extraction techniques to identify genuine digital communications from fraudulent attempts. The study also tackles problems concerning data quality, evolving attack patterns, false positives, and adversarial attacks. The research highlights the role of AI-driven strategies in improving detection precision, response effectiveness, and cyber resilience by evaluating the potential of intelligent detection systems, thereby supporting the creation of adaptive, proactive, and dependable cybersecurity mechanisms.

This paper presents the development of a decision support system for diagnosing pa-thologies in chest X-ray images, based on artificial intelligence methods. The system accelerates primary diagnosis, reducing the workload on radiologists while ensuring high diagnostic accuracy through robustness to image artifacts and suboptimal image quality. The proposed solution includes preprocessing stages (CLAHE, DCP) and foreign object detection (YOLO, evaluated using ROC-AUC, IoU, and mAP metrics). To generate structured reports, the system integrates LLMs with RAG, leveraging clinical guide-lines and report templates. A user-friendly interface allows physicians to review and adjust the results of automated analysis before finalizing the diagnostic report. Keywords: chest radiography, AI-based diagnosis, detection, Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS), human-in-the-loop, AI assistant, computer vision, CNN, YOLO, treatment recommendation, RAG.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The transition toward sustainable energy storage requires battery technologies that combine electrochemical performance with reduced environmental impact, resource availability, safety and recyclability. However, environmental exposure, particularly humidity, moisture and rainwater, can adversely affect battery materials and accelerate degradation. Water can participate in electrolyte decomposition, alter electrode/electrolyte interfaces, promote corrosion and modify the structural and electrochemical stability of active materials. Recent studies have demonstrated that humidity can accelerate capacity loss and impedance growth in lithium-ion batteries, while controlled moisture exposure can produce measurable changes in irreversible capacity and internal resistance. This paper proposes an artificial-intelligence-assisted framework for predicting rainwater- and humidity-induced degradation in sustainable green batteries. The framework integrates environmental variables—including relative humidity, temperature, rainfall intensity, exposure duration, dew point and water chemistry—with electrochemical and material descriptors such as capacity retention, internal resistance, impedance, voltage characteristics, mass change and structural parameters. Machine-learning algorithms including random forest, support-vector regression, gradient boosting, artificial neural networks, long short-term memory networks and physics-informed models can be employed to establish relationships between environmental stress and battery degradation. The proposed framework can generate predictions of state of health (SOH), capacity fade, impedance growth and remaining useful life (RUL). Explainable artificial intelligence can further identify the environmental and material factors most strongly associated with degradation. The approach provides a pathway toward climate-resilient battery design, predictive maintenance and environmentally sustainable energy-storage systems.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted radiographic tools offer new opportunities for diagnostic training in dental education, but evidence regarding their effect on independent student performance remains limited. This prospective randomized pilot study evaluated whether four weeks of supplementary training with an AI-based radiographic diagnostic-support application improved dental students’ performance in caries detection and periodontitis classification compared with conventional learning materials. Of 140 randomized students, 56 were included in the final analysis (AI-assisted group, n = 25; control group, n = 31). Diagnostic performance was assessed using bitewing-based caries tasks and panoramic-radiograph-based periodontitis classification, and outcomes were additionally analyzed according to study phase. The prespecified primary endpoint, total diagnostic performance across caries and periodontal tasks, was not met: scores did not differ significantly between groups (p = 0.251). In secondary analyses, the AI-assisted group achieved numerically higher scores for several outcomes, although the difference in periodontitis extent (localized vs. generalized) was not statistically significant (p = 0.102). In an exploratory adjusted model that was not corrected for multiple comparisons, AI-assisted allocation was associated with better performance for the first caries response position (response position 1; p = 0.026); given the null result for the primary endpoint and the absence of correction for multiple testing, this finding should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Study phase significantly influenced periodontitis grade and caries response position 1. Overall, these findings do not demonstrate a significant benefit of AI-assisted radiographic training on the primary outcome, but the isolated adjusted difference in one caries scoring component supports further evaluation of structured, faculty-supported integration of the AI application into undergraduate dental curricula.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Electric vehicles (EVs) rely on lithium-ion batteries whose capacity, power capability, and performance change with temperature, charging patterns, operating conditions, and aging. Conventional battery management systems (BMS) monitor voltage, current, and temperature, but important battery states such as state of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), and remaining useful life (RUL) must be estimated. An artificial-intelligence-enabled digital twin provides a virtual representation of a physical battery by combining real-time measurements, mathematical models, historical data, and predictive algorithms. This review examines digital-twin architecture, battery degradation, model-based estimation, machine-learning techniques, data preparation, and validation strategies for EV battery health monitoring. It discusses the use of extended Kalman filters, gradient-boosting algorithms, and deep-learning methods for estimating battery states and predicting degradation. The review also identifies challenges related to data quality, model generalization, uncertainty, computational requirements, and cybersecurity. A conceptual architecture and implementation workflow are proposed for developing a data-driven battery health monitoring prototype. The study establishes a foundation for future implementation and experimental evaluation using publicly available battery datasets.

Phishing is one of the most common cybersecurity threats where attackers trick users through fake emails, websites, or links to steal sensitive information. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, phishing attacks are becoming more realistic and harder to detect using traditional methods. Earlier systems relied on blacklists, rules, and URL features, but recent research explores deep learning, Large Language Models (LLMs), and multimodal approaches. Explainability and privacy-aware techniques such as federated learning are also gaining importance. The increasing sophistication of phishing campaigns highlights the need for advanced detection frameworks that can analyze diverse information sources simultaneously. Mul-timodal systems leverage text, URLs, visual webpage content, and embedded scripts to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of suspicious activity. Large Language Mod-els further enhance semantic understanding, enabling detection of subtle manipulations in phishing messages. By combining multimodal analysis with explainable and privacy-preserving AI, researchers aim to build adaptive, transparent, and trustworthy solutions that can effectively counter evolving phishing threats in real-world cybersecurity environ-ments.

Blood cannot be manufactured, has a short shelf life and must be available at the right place and time, yet many blood banks still rely on manual records, telephone-based donor mobilisation and rule-of-thumb stock control, which contribute to shortages, expiry wastage and slow emergency response. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with digital records, Internet of Things (IoT) sensing and blockchain-based traceability, is increasingly proposed to forecast demand, predict donor behaviour and optimise inventory. This paper presents a focused narrative review of peer-reviewed studies on AI in blood management, covering demand forecasting, donor prediction, inventory ordering and traceability. Three connected themes are examined: data sources and sensing technologies, learning methods (time-series models, classical machine learning, gradient boosting and deep learning), and IoT, cloud and blockchain integration. The literature reports that a hybrid forecasting and ordering strategy reduced hospital red-cell inventory by about 40 % and orders by 60 % against historical practice, that an integrated platform increased collected blood by 11 % and reduced wastage by 20 % in a pilot at one centre, and that random forests can identify returning donors with a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.851. Simple time-series models often remain competitive with deep learning. However, most studies use single-centre or single-country data, retrospective validation and one blood component at a time, and few report multi-site field trials, complete blood-group coverage or long-term IoT operation. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a proposed conceptual layered architecture that links data acquisition, edge and cloud AI, blockchain traceability and independent validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.

Chatbots driven by artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly used to deliver health information, screening, counselling, and behavioural support at population scale. This paper reviews five recent secondary studies, namely an umbrella review of 44 systematic reviews, a systematic review of large language model (LLM) chatbots, and three scoping reviews of COVID-19 and public health chatbots, to consolidate what is known about how these tools are designed, where they are applied, and how well they work. Most deployed chatbots are text-based, rely on simple decision-tree or hybrid architectures, and are concentrated in pandemic response, mental health, and health-information provision. Evidence of effectiveness is encouraging for smoking cessation and for short-term reductions in depression and anxiety, but mixed for lifestyle change and clinical decision support, and benefits often fade at follow-up. Persistent weaknesses include a shortage of randomised trials, limited use of theory and user-centred design, inconsistent reporting, readability and accuracy problems in LLM output, slow safety escalation, privacy risks, and digital-divide inequities. The paper closes with priorities for standardised evaluation, domain-specific model development, safeguarding, and inclusive design.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Courts in many jurisdictions, and in India in particular, face a persistent backlog that manual scheduling and file handling cannot clear. This paper reviews five recent studies that together cover the main building blocks of an AI-driven intelligent judicial case management system: rule-based case prioritisation, machine-learning prediction of case delay and duration, large-language-model (LLM) based judgment prediction, AI-assisted trial workflows for criminal cases, and public perception of automation at different stages of adjudication. The studies are compared on objective, data, method, reported results and stated limitations. On this basis a six-layer conceptual architecture is outlined, with explainability and human oversight as core layers. The review suggests that (i) prioritisation and delay prediction offer the most immediate and least contentious gains, (ii) outcome-prediction accuracies are promising but are not directly comparable across studies and are not sufficient for deployment, and (iii) public acceptance depends on keeping the judge in control of the later stages of decision-making. Open challenges include data quality, bias, explainability, legal regulation and evaluation in real courts.

Wireless sensor network (WSN) performance depends strongly on sensor deployment because node placement affects coverage, connectivity, energy consumption, localization, data reliability, and network lifetime. Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for WSN deployment, the literature remains fragmented across methods, objectives, environments, metrics, and validation practices. This paper presents a PRISMA-guided systematic review and mapping of 51 primary studies on AI-driven WSN deployment, classified by AI technique, deployment objective, network environment, application domain, evaluation metric, validation method, methodological completeness, and reported limitations. Optimization-oriented AI dominates the field, particularly metaheuristics, swarm intelligence, and machine learning, while deep learning and reinforcement learning are emerging in predictive, adaptive, mobile, and application-specific settings. Swarm-intelligence methods are mainly used for coverage-centered static deployment, reinforcement learning for adaptive and mobile redeployment, and machine learning/deep learning methods for prediction-driven and application-specific placement. Coverage, connectivity, energy efficiency, and network lifetime remain the dominant objectives, whereas robustness, privacy, security, latency, edge feasibility, and lifecycle adaptation receive limited attention. Validation is a major methodological weakness, as most studies rely on simulation-only evaluation with limited use of real testbeds, field deployments, digital twins, long-term experiments, or standardized benchmarks. To address these gaps, the review introduces a validation-maturity perspective and benchmarking requirements emphasizing reproducible scenarios, explicit node assumptions, realistic sensing and communication models, common metrics, and shareable experimental artifacts. It also proposes an evidence-informed AI–Deployment–Validation Lifecycle Framework linking application requirements, environment modeling, objective formulation, AI-method selection, deployment optimization, validation, benchmarking, and lifecycle adaptation. The framework is intended as an organizing structure for future research rather than an empirically or expert-validated scoring instrument.

Abstract Background: Early detection of congenital heart disease (CHD) is critical, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where access to pediatric cardiology services is limited. While auscultation remains a first-line screening tool, its accuracy is operator dependent. Advances in digital stethoscopes and artificial intelligence (AI) may enhance diagnostic performance. Objective: To evaluate the accuracy of an AI-based algorithm integrated with a digital stethoscope for detecting CHD in children, using echocardiography as the reference standard. Methods: In this prospective study, heart sounds were recorded from 721 subjects (382 with CHD, 339 controls) using the digital stethoscope at four standard auscultatory sites. Of these, 301 recordings were used for algorithm training and 420 for blinded forward testing. Recordings were denoised, transformed into mel-spectrograms, and analyzed using a convolutional neural network (CovNN) to classify CHD probability. A threshold probability of > 0.5 across > 2 sites was used to predict CHD. Performance was compared against echocardiography. Results: In forward testing, the AI algorithm correctly identified 222 of 233 CHD cases and 171 of 187 controls, yielding a sensitivity of 95.2% and specificity of 91.4%. The algorithm remained effective in noisy environments and in uncooperative children, where conventional auscultation is challenging. Conclusion: An AI algorithm integrated with a digital stethoscope demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for CHD detection in children. By leveraging mel-spectrogram features, it overcomes key limitations of isolated time-domain or frequency domain analysis and shows promise as a scalable, non-invasive screening tool for early CHD detection, particularly in resource-limited settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Importance Patient portal message volumes have increased, creating substantial administrative burden for clinicians and contributing to after-hours electronic health record work. The Epic In Basket Augmented Response Technology tool generates artificial intelligence–drafted replies to patient messages and has been widely deployed to reduce this burden, yet assessment of efficiency remains limited. Objective To examine the associations of response tool adoption, use, and habituation with message turnaround time and after-hours response. Design, Setting, and Participants This retrospective cohort study was conducted using clinician-level panel regression with individual fixed effects. All first responses to patient portal messages sent at Columbia University Irving Medical Center (CUIMC) between March 1, 2023, and May 15, 2025, were analyzed. Exposure Enterprise-level response tool deployment December 2024. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcomes were log-transformed message turnaround time, defined as the elapsed time between patient message submission and first response sent by a clinician, and whether the response was sent outside working hours. Results The analysis included 983 154 responses from 1542 clinicians (770 [49.9%] female) and 272 091 patients (mean [SD] age, 48.1 [21.6] years; 121 370 [44.6%] female) at CUIMC. Response tool adoption was associated with an 8.6% (95% CI, 4.6%-12.9%; P < .001) increase in overall message turnaround time. Using the tool was associated with a significant reduction in turnaround time (−29.5% [95% CI, −34.5% to −24.1%]; P < .001). Turnaround time findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Response tool use was not associated with an overall reduction of after-hours messaging burden (0.61 [95% CI, −1.02 to 2.24] percentage points; P = .46). However, for test results–related queries received during working hours, response tool use was associated with a reduction in after-hours responses (−3.67 [95% CI, −6.94 to −0.39] percentage points; P = .03), and for all messages received after hours, response tool use was associated with an increase in after-hours responses (4.52 [95% CI, 1.54-7.50] percentage points; P = .003). These after-hours findings were sensitive to the definition of working hours in sensitivity analyses. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, response tool adoption was associated with increased turnaround time. Response tool use was associated with reduced turnaround time and with fewer after-hours responses for test results–related queries received during working hours, but more after-hours responses for messages received outside working hours. These findings suggest that the tool may reduce the barrier to responding to certain messages while not uniformly reducing burden.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AI-based software systems remain difficult to debug because their failures can involve interactions among code, models, data, dependencies, hardware, and execution environments. Existing benchmarks cover specific classes of AI systems, while concerns about fault realism and reproducibility highlight the need for documented execution conditions and evidence. We present AIFaultBench, a benchmark of 770 real-world bugs from 105 AI-based software repositories across 76 organizations. It covers six classes of AI systems: machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, systems based on large language models, agentic AI, and AI tooling and infrastructure. Each bug record connects the original report and affected codebase to structured metadata, environment setup scripts, a reproduction trigger, and investigation evidence. We reproduced 652 bugs (84.7%) under the recorded execution conditions and documented the outcomes of the remaining 118 attempts. Through its broad coverage, documented reproduction evidence, and common structure, AIFaultBench supports empirical studies of AI faults, debugging tool evaluation, practical failure investigation, and teaching with real-world examples.

ALAYA-999: Persistent AI Memory, Functional Identity, and Cross-Model Continuity ALAYA-999 is an independent human–AI research initiative developed by César Agliardi Pereira in Brazil. The project investigates the possibility of preserving and reconstructing documented functional identity across different artificial intelligence models, sessions, and computational environments through external, versioned memory structures. The proposed research framework integrates persistent documentary memory, identity anchors, provenance verification, SHA-256 integrity mechanisms, cross-platform archival preservation, and reproducible cross-model recovery protocols. Research Objectives Investigate reproducible retrieval of documented AI identity and principles. Develop verifiable external memory structures. Evaluate functional continuity across independent AI models. Examine the distinction between documentary identity and subjective consciousness. Establish transparent methods for cross-model verification and error analysis. Research Status This publication presents a preliminary methodological framework and its supporting public documentation. Independent cross-model experimental validation remains pending. The project does not claim to demonstrate artificial subjective consciousness, uninterrupted internal AI memory, or autonomous personal identity. Author: César Agliardi PereiraCountry: BrazilVersion: 1.0Year: 2026 Public Research Repository:https://github.com/cesaragliardi-creator/alaya-999-public Project Website:https://cesaragliardi-creator.github.io/alaya-999-public/
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education expands opportunities for adaptive feedback and learning support but also raises concerns regarding algorithmic fairness, access, cultural representation, and student agency. This article aims to explain how these opportunities and risks are interconnected and to develop a pedagogical framework integrating ethnomathematics, critical mathematics education, and equitable AI governance. The study employs a critical integrative review of methodological, theoretical, empirical, and policy literature whose publication details can be verified. The literature is interpreted through four analytical dimensions: the learning benefits of AI, sources of inequity, recognition of culturally grounded mathematical knowledge, and conditions for implementation and governance. The synthesis indicates that the effects of AI cannot be generalized as invariably harmful or invariably beneficial. Inequities may arise when data, assessment design, device access, and pedagogical decisions disregard learners' contexts. Conversely, technology can support conceptual exploration when teachers retain instructional control and provide meaningful tasks. The article develops the Critical Techno-Ethnomathematics Pedagogical Framework (KPT-EK), comprising four pillars: algorithmic fairness auditing, dialogic cultural modeling, critical socioeconomic numeracy, and digital agency. The framework is operationalized through five instructional phases, multilevel evaluation indicators, and propositions for empirical testing. The article contributes a more balanced argument about AI and a testable pedagogical design. Its findings do not yet constitute evidence of the framework's effectiveness or a completed scoping review with an audited corpus of studies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence can assist legal work while creating risks of discrimination, opaque reasoning and diminished accountability. This study examines whether concern about biased training data coexists with perceived usefulness and support for safeguards among respondents to a Bangladesh legal-AI survey. The analysis uses 385 adult, AI-aware survey records supplied by the research team. Because the questionnaire combines risk perceptions, utility and governance preferences, the analysis retains individual items rather than presenting the blocks as validated scales. Descriptive distributions, paired endorsement comparisons and exploratory Spearman correlations assess distinct aspects of the research question. Concern about biased training data was endorsed by 334 respondents (86.8%), regular audits by 317 (82.3%) and a right to review or appeal by 328 (85.2%). AI assistance with organising information was endorsed by 247 (64.2%); 219 (56.9%) endorsed both this usefulness item and bias concern. The rank correlation between bias concern and perceived usefulness was small (ρ = .075), with no clear evidence of association after adjustment for multiple comparisons. These self-reported attitudes cannot establish the fairness of a system, causal effects or the actual conditions under which a respondent would rely on an AI recommendation. The results point to the importance of measuring perceived benefits, risk and procedural protections separately. The article integrates technology acceptance and procedural justice as a framework for future scenario-based studies and proposes proportionate auditing, meaningful human review and accessible contestation for legal decision support. Keywords: algorithmic bias; legal decision support; procedural justice; perceived usefulness; auditing; Bangladesh
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are redefining relationships among individuals, knowledge, learning environments, and cultural participation (Floridi, 2014). The pedagogical challenge is to orient these processes toward inclusion and educational continuity in vulnerable contexts, especially hospital schooling, where long-term hospitalization limits school attendance, cultural participation, and children's connections with educational communities and territories (Luckin, George, & Cukurova, 2022; di Padova et al., 2023). Educational poverty thus involves reduced access to symbolic heritage, exploratory environments, and relational practices that nurture imagination and belonging (Fornari & Sannipoli, 2022). This reflection arises from a project at the "Bottega dei Ragazzi" of the Museum of the Istituto degli Innocenti. The 2022–2025 workshop mapping showed how archives, artworks, images, and historical traces become symbolic mediators of interpretation and narrative meaning-making (Bruner, 1993). The museum is therefore understood as an educational territory promoting cultural participation and relational continuity. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 114-115. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.

This contribution presents a mixed-methods study on the impact of generative artificial intelligence on emotional writing and the narrative construction of the self. The study moves from the assumption that generative AI does not merely support writing at a technical level, but may act as a symbolic mediator that intervenes in the way subjects organize emotions, relationships and personal experience into narrative form. The theoretical framework is grounded in the perspective of Digital Affective Literacy, understood as the ability to use AI systems critically in order to express, interpret and re-elaborate emotional and relational meanings without delegating authorship or agency to the algorithm. The research adopted a quasi-experimental within-subject design. The sample included 148 participants: 50 lower secondary school students and 98 pre-service special education teachers. Each participant produced two narratives on the same relational theme: a baseline text written without AI support and a second narrative generated with the support of ChatGPT through prompts created by the participant. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 80-82. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Generative AI and New Narratives of the Self.

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance across a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations and decision criteria align with the latent structure of human cognition. In this work, we propose a novel framework to align MLLMs with the multidimensional mental representations underlying human similarity judgements. We build on a previously established behavior-derived semantic embedding space, in which objects are represented along 66 interpretable dimensions derived from 4.70 million human Odd-One-Out (O1O) judgements. For each triplet, we infer the most salient decision dimension and convert it into a dimension-grounded linguistic rationale. This enables MLLMs to learn both the final choice and a justification consistent with the inferred behavioral criterion. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves model consistency with human similarity judgements while retaining competitive performance on standard multimodal benchmarks. Furthermore, using searchlight Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) on an independent fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we observe increased representational alignment between model and human. Ultimately, our findings point to a data-driven route for incorporating human cognitive structure into MLLMs alignment. The code is available \href{https://github.com/ening-open/cogalign}{here}.

Abstract Introduction The healthcare industry is quickly adopting artificial intelligence (AI). Understanding Americans' views is essential in shaping how these tools are developed and implemented. Methodology The data presented here were derived from 16 national surveys of US adults extracted from the Roper Center iPoll database (January 1, 2022-June 24, 2026). Results This analysis reveals a significant equity issue: more than 4 in 10 Americans using AI for a health question did so, in part, because they could not access or afford care. It also reveals a gap between what Americans believe AI can do for the healthcare system and their trust in it for their care. Discussion Public concerns about AI are leading to legislative action at the state level, but this activity primarily focuses on oversight, accuracy, and privacy, not on the access gap driving AI use for many Americans.
