documents.abstract: Cybersickness is a major challenge to the reliable use of augmented reality (AR) systems, as it can impair operators’ cognition and task performance. However, existing cybersickness models primarily rely on predictive approaches and lack formally verifiable methods to assess cybersickness and its impact on task performance. This paper introduces a formal modeling approach using Discrete-Time Markov Chains (DTMC) to represent the temporal progression of cybersickness and its impact on task performance in a checkpoint surveillance scenario. The model incorporates exposure duration as a key cybersickness-inducing factor and uses preliminary experimental data to generate mock datasets for model construction and verification. The model enables probabilistic verification of properties, such as bounds on the onset of cybersickness and task performance. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of applying formal methods to model human interaction with AR systems and to generate probabilistic guarantees on operators’ cybersickness and task performance.

Tourism contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions. This study developed a trip-level carbon prediction framework for community-based tourism, serving as a surrogate model for activity-based carbon accounting equations. To prevent target leakage, predictor features were restricted to 34 pre-travel proxies, excluding post-travel parameters. Five machine learning algorithms, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, eXtreme Gradient Boosting, Light Gradient-Boosting Machine, and Categorical Boosting, were evaluated using 13,000 synthetic trip profiles generated from 650 empirical baseline respondents (partitioned into 10,400 development scenarios from 520 respondents and 2600 hold-out scenarios from 130 respondents). LINE Mini App provided instantaneous carbon estimations and personalized recommendations. Categorical Boosting achieved predictive performance, with a mean absolute error of 1.28 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent (kgCO2e), root mean square error of 1.96 kgCO2e, mean absolute percentage error of 6.90%, and coefficient of determination of 0.948, outperforming linear baselines. Explainable Artificial Intelligence using SHapley Additive exPlanations indicated that the model captures primary pre-travel drivers, led by travel distance, stay duration, travel budget, and travel planning score. External field evaluation: 105 independent cohort users generated 1297 recommendation impressions, 688 clicks, and 347 acceptances, achieving a 53.05% click-through rate, a 50.44% acceptance rate, a 247.64 ms mean response time, and an 86.40% user feedback score, supporting proactive decision choice architecture for sustainable community-based tourism.

Abstract Early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma is critical to preserve access to curative treatment options. The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) provides a standardized framework for non-invasive diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, based on major visual imaging features. However, these features may be difficult to assess consistently, particularly in small liver lesions. We developed dLI-RADS, an interpretable artificial intelligence method designed to estimate the probability of hepatocellular carcinoma from multiphase computed tomography images of manually segmented liver lesions, while remaining aligned with LI-RADS-related imaging concepts. dLI-RADS combines neural network-derived predictions with handcrafted quantitative imaging measurements reflecting LI-RADS major features and integrates these inputs using logistic regression. In this multicenter retrospective study, patients with multiphase computed tomography and at least one liver lesion were included, while lesions larger than 40 mm were excluded. Histology served as the reference standard for hepatocellular carcinoma, and a composite reference standard was used for non-hepatocellular carcinoma lesions. The lesion-level accuracy of dLI-RADS and LI-RADS were compared on the internal evaluation set using 10,000-repetition bootstrap non-inferiority tests, with 5% margins and significance levels. On the external test set, sensitivities were similarly compared. A total of 143 (61 years ± 9, 125 men), 62 (61y ± 10, 49 men), and 133 (59y ± 10, 103 men) patients with 196, 84, and 171 lesions (mean diameter 17.7, 18.3, and 21.8 millimeters) were respectively included in the training, internal and external evaluation sets. dLI-RADS was non-inferior to LI-RADS for lesion-level accuracy in the internal evaluation set, achieving 80% accuracy compared with 74% for LI-RADS ( p = 0.04). On the external evaluation set, dLI-RADS achieved a sensitivity of 93% compared with 78% for LI-RADS (non-inferiority p < 0.001). On this same set, dLI-RADS also achieved 74% specificity, 86% accuracy, and an AUC of 84%. Because LI-RADS features were unavailable for non-HCC lesions, only sensitivity could be directly compared between dLI-RADS and LI-RADS. These findings suggest that dLI-RADS may provide interpretable decision support for hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosis on multiphase computed tomography, particularly for small liver lesions.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Non-ergonomic working postures may increase the risk of musculoskeletal disorders, particularly in jobs involving manual activities, trunk bending, and repetitive movements. This study aims to identify and classify working-posture risks and formulate ergonomic improvement recommendations for site workers at PT Prima Sarana Gemilang. A descriptive approach was applied through observations of 15 work activities. Postures were assessed using the Ovako Working Posture Analysis System (OWAS), which classifies posture based on back position, arm position, leg position, and handled load. The results showed that six activities (40%) were classified as risk category 1, three activities (20%) as category 2, and six activities (40%) as category 3. No activities were classified as category 4. These findings indicate that several work activities require improvements in posture and working conditions. Recommended interventions include adjusting workstation height, providing material-handling aids, improving work methods, scheduling adequate rest periods, and providing ergonomic training. The findings are expected to support the prioritization of ergonomic interventions in the workplace.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Low Back Pain (LBP) is a disease caused by non-ergonomic working conditions during manual handling activities. LBP is a leading cause of activity limitations, disability, inability and absenteeism from work. The aim of this study was to analyze ergonomic risk factors for LBP complaints and their relationship to the two in charcoal briquette manufacturing industry workers at PT. Arkelindo Bara Sejahtera. This study was quantitative with a cross-sectional approach. The study was conducted from June to November 2025. The population and sample were 183 and 151 workers, respectively. Research data was obtained from questionnaires, interviews, diagnoses, and direct on-site observations. Data analysis was conducted using univariate, bivariate, and multivariate methods. The results showed that as many as 64.2% of participants experienced complaints of severe LBP. It was also found that awkward postures, static work positions, repetitive movements and excessive force use were at risk of 62.9%, 70.2%, 73.5% and 57.6%, respectively. There is a relationship between awkward postures (p = 0.023, OR = 2.843), static work positions (p =0.004, OR = 3.875), repetitive movements (p = 0.000, OR = 6.013) and excessive force use (p = 0.003, OR = 4.178) and NBP complaints. The dominant ergonomic risk factor for LBP complaints is repetitive movements with an OR value of 6.013. This study indicates that repeated exposure to sitting or standing for more than half the working day, combined with awkward postures such as bending and twisting, were the dominant contributing factors to LBP. It is hoped that companies can implement ergonomic work positions to ensure worker comfort. Keywords: Charcoal Briquette Industry, Ergonomic Risks, Back Pain, Occupational Health. ABSTRAK Nyeri punggung bawah (NPB) merupakan penyakit akibat kondisi kerja yang tidak ergonomis selama aktivitas manual handling. NPB merupakan salah satu penyebab utama keterbatasan aktivitas, kecacatan, ketidakmampuan dan ketidakhadiran dalam bekerja. Tujuan penelitian ini adalah untuk menganalisis faktor risiko ergonomi terhadap keluhan NPB dan hubungan keduanya pada pekerja industri pembuatan briket arang di PT. Arkelindo Bara Sejahtera.Jenis penelitian ini adalah kuantitatif dengan pendekatan cross-sectional. Penelitian dilaksanakan bulan Juni hingga November 2025. Populasi dan sampel berturut-turut adalah 183 dan 151 pekerja. Data penelitian diperoleh dari kuesioner, wawancara, diagnosa dan pengamatan langsung. Analisis data dilakukan secara univariat, bivariat dan multivariat. Hasil menunjukkan bahwa sebanyak 64,2% responden mengalami keluhan NPB berat. Itu ditemukan juga bahwa postur tubuh janggal, posisi kerja statis, gerakan berulang, dan penggunaan tenaga berlebihan masing-masing berisiko sebesar 62,9%, 70,2%, 73,5%, dan 57,6%. Terdapat hubungan antara postur tubuh yang tidak nyaman (p = 0,023, OR = 2,843), posisi kerja statis (p = 0,004, OR = 3,875), gerakan berulang (p = 0,000, OR = 6,013), dan penggunaan tenaga berlebihan (p = 0,003, OR = 4,178) dengan keluhan NPB. Faktor risiko ergonomi dominan terhadap keluhan NPB adalah pergerakan berulang dengan nilai OR 6,013. Penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa paparan berulang terhadap posisi duduk atau berdiri selama lebih dari setengah hari kerja, dikombinasikan dengan postur tubuh janggal seperti membungkuk dan memutar badan, merupakan faktor utama penyebab NPB. Itu diharapkan bahwa perusahaan dapat menerapkan posisi kerja ergonomis agar pekerja nyaman saat bekerja. Kata Kunci: Industri Briket Arang, Risiko Ergonomi, Nyeri Punggung, Kesehatan Kerja.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose This study addresses a knowledge gap by showing how perceived software quality dimensions extracted from user-generated reviews influence user satisfaction in mobile banking applications. The paper extends existing theory by demonstrating how sentiment polarity moderates the relationship between perceived software quality dimensions and user ratings across both fully digital and hybrid digital–physical banks. Design/methodology/approach A large corpus of online reviews was analysed using a hybrid text-mining approach that integrates latent dirichlet allocation (LDA), sentiment analysis, large language model–assisted topic interpretation and sentence-BERT (SBERT) semantic similarity modelling. User-derived attributes were mapped to the software quality dimensions defined in ISO/IEC 25010:2023, resulting in a framework that operationalises perceived software quality. Regression analysis estimated their functional and emotional effects on user ratings. Findings Functional suitability, interaction capability and maintainability positively impact user satisfaction, while performance efficiency, reliability, flexibility, safety and security issues primarily drive dissatisfaction. Compatibility shows no significant effect. Sentiment polarity moderates these associations: under positive sentiment, negative quality effects intensify, while the moderation of positive effects varies across dimensions. Originality/value A novel framework based on ISO/IEC 25010:2023 is used to assess the perceived service quality of mobile banking applications for digital-only and banks with physical branches, by analysing user sentiment in online reviews. Further, the work examines the effect of perceived software quality on user satisfaction, specifically how this varies with sentiment polarity. The relationship between software quality and user satisfaction is found to be asymmetric and conditioned by review sentiment. Under positive sentiment, negatively associated quality dimensions exert stronger adverse effects on satisfaction, while positive effects vary across dimensions. Quality-satisfaction estimates must account for this asymmetric sentiment moderation. Two novel visualisation tools capture how quality dimensions differ in their impact, prominence and sentiment in shaping user satisfaction.

The Social Security Administration for Employment (BPJS Ketenagakerjaan) recorded 234,370 occupational accident cases in 2021, increasing to 265,334 cases in 2022. In 2023, the number of occupational accidents rose further to 370,747 cases, and in 2024 it increased to 462,241 cases. Based on the latest data from the Ministry of Manpower (Kemnaker), 47,300 cases were reported as of April 2025. The construction sector contributes most to occupational accidents, accounting for about 32% of cases annually. In response, it is necessary to identify potential occupational accident risks and determine which occur most frequently. This study focuses on a bridge duplication construction project. The research uses the Delphi method, in which several Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) experts provide input on potential occupational accident risks to validate the risk variables through consensus. The study then used Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) to identify the most dominant occupational accident risks. The Delphi method identified that, out of 31 occupational accident risks, 29 were validated as potential risks through expert consensus. The FMEA results further indicated that, of the 29 potential risks, 4 occupational accident risks were the most dominant. This study's results are expected to serve as a reference for stakeholders to identify potential occupational accident risks and determine which are most prevalent.

Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in the garment sector, particularly home-based convection industries, contribute significantly to local employment in Gresik City, Indonesia. However, the informal nature of these enterprises, limited workspace, and minimal occupational safety management may expose workers to substantial occupational hazards that are rarely assessed systematically. This study aimed to identify potential workplace hazards, evaluate their risk levels, and determine appropriate risk control strategies using the Hazard Identification, Risk Assessment, and Determining Control (HIRADC) method integrated with a phenomenological approach. A qualitative phenomenological design was employed involving 45 workers from 10 garment home Industri SMEs in Gresik City. Data were collected through structured field observations, in-depth semi-structured interviews, and contextual workplace assessment checklists. Risk evaluation was conducted using the HIRADC matrix by determining Likelihood (L), Severity (S), and Risk (R = L × S). Data analysis included thematic coding, phenomenological reduction, and integration of qualitative findings with quantitative risk scores. The dominant hazards identified were ergonomic risks (prolonged static posture and repetitive motion), mechanical hazards (needle punctures and cutting injuries), thermal hazards (burns from ironing), and electrical and fire hazards due to overloaded outlets and combustible material accumulation. HIRADC analysis revealed that ergonomic risks (R=15), burn injuries (R=16), and fire hazards (R=15) were categorized as high risk, while mechanical and housekeeping hazards were classified as moderate to high risk. Phenomenologically, workers tended to normalize physical discomfort and prioritize productivity over safety, perceiving occupational safety as an individual responsibility rather than a systematic management issue. The findings indicate that home-based garment SMEs possess significant occupational risks that require structured yet contextually feasible risk management strategies. Integrating phenomenological insights with HIRADC provides both experiential understanding and objective prioritization, supporting the development of realistic, low-cost hierarchical control interventions for sustainable occupational safety improvement. Keywords: Garment SMEs, Hazard Identification, HIRADC, Occupational Risk, Occupational Safety and Health.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Web agents are increasingly deployed to complete tasks autonomously on real websites, where adversarially injected content can induce them to perform unauthorized actions. Existing evaluations primarily use fixed attacks or focus on a single attack type, and evaluate attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, thus underestimating how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks. To address the gap, we introduce REEF, a benchmark of red-teaming executable environments with faithful verification for measuring the security vulnerabilities of web agents. REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites spanning travel, commerce, productivity, media, and communication, and pairs every authentic benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and the environment level. REEF's state-based verifiers provide the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, an adaptive near-miss-guided lure evolution framework for red-teaming. Rather than evaluating a fixed attack set, ANGLER uses outcomes from prior rollouts to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds during refinement. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate (ASR) of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Compared with attack-free execution on the same benign tasks, attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate (BSR) from 61.9% to 44.4%.

RESUMO A incorporação da Inteligência Artificial (IA) na gestão da Saúde e Segurança do Trabalho (SST) amplia a identificação de perigos, o monitoramento ambiental e a análise preditiva de acidentes. Contudo, traz desafios técnicos, éticos e jurídicos sobre a confiabilidade dos dados e a responsabilidade profissional. Este estudo analisou criticamente o uso da IA no gerenciamento de riscos ocupacionais, mapeando suas oportunidades, limitações e impactos na atuação do Engenheiro de Segurança do Trabalho. Trata-se de uma revisão integrativa da literatura de natureza aplicada e abordagem qualitativa. Os resultados indicam que a IA possui elevado potencial analítico e operacional, mas apresenta riscos como alucinações, viés de automação e dependência da qualidade dos dados. Como contribuição, o estudo propõe um Framework de Governança pautado na supervisão humana obrigatória, validação técnica, transparência e responsabilidade profissional preservada sob supervisão humana. Conclui-se que a IA deve atuar estritamente como ferramenta de apoio, mantendo o protagonismo e a responsabilidade legal do especialista no processo decisório Palavras-chave: Inteligência Artificial. Engenharia de Segurança do Trabalho. Gestão de Riscos Ocupacionais. Prevenção de Acidentes. Governança da Inteligência Artificial. Responsabilidade Técnica. ABSTRACT The adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) management enhances hazard identification, environmental monitoring, and accident prediction. However, it raises technical, ethical, and legal challenges regarding data reliability and professional accountability. This study critically analyzed AI applications in occupational risk management, identifying opportunities, limitations, and impacts on Safety Engineers' technical responsibility. Developed as a qualitative, applied integrative literature review, the findings highlight AI's strong potential for data processing and continuous monitoring alongside critical limitations such as hallucinations, automation bias, and data dependency. As a primary contribution, the study proposes a Governance Framework based on mandatory human oversight, technical validation, algorithmic transparency, and non-transferable professional responsibility. It is concluded that AI must serve strictly as a decision-support tool, preserving the central role and legal responsibility of safety professionals. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence. Safety Engineering. Occupational Risk Management. Accident Prevention. Artificial Intelligence Governance. Technical Responsibility.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The article examines the possibilities of using artificial intelligence in the system of accounting and analytical support for managing crop production and export operations. The relevance of the study is associated with the growing amount of accounting, production, logistics and foreign economic information that agribusiness enterprises need to process, particularly under the unstable conditions of the Ukrainian economy. The study identifies the main areas of AI application for automating accounting procedures, analyzing production costs, inventories and revenues, forecasting production indicators, detecting deviations, and supporting management decisions. Particular attention is paid to linking accounting data with information on crop yields, resource consumption, inventories, logistics, export contracts, settlements with counterparties and foreign currency transactions. Such integration provides a more complete basis for assessing production efficiency, determining the causes of changes in costs and financial results, and responding to deviations in a timely manner. An approach to integrating AI tools into the accounting and analytical system of agribusiness enterprises is proposed, taking into account the specific conditions of agricultural production and export activity in Ukraine. The study also considers the use of AI for processing primary and export documents, identifying inconsistencies between accounting and operational data, forecasting production costs and yields, and assessing the possible impact of logistics changes on export results. The main benefits and risks of AI use are outlined, including dependence on data quality, protection of confidential information, possible algorithmic errors, and excessive reliance on automated recommendations. It is emphasized that AI should complement rather than replace accounting procedures and professional judgement. The proposed approach can be used as a basis for further improvement of digital accounting and analytical systems in Ukrainian agribusiness enterprises and for strengthening information support for production and export management.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare by enabling precision, predictive, and person-centered approaches that enhance the quality, accessibility, and efficiency of nursing care. Community, mental, and child health nursing are increasingly benefiting from AI-driven innovations, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, clinical decision support systems, wearable technologies, conversational AI, and telehealth platforms. These technologies facilitate early disease detection, population health surveillance, risk prediction, personalized interventions, remote patient monitoring, developmental screening, mental health assessment, and evidence-based clinical decision-making. This narrative review synthesizes contemporary evidence on the integration of AI across community, mental, and child health nursing and explores its implications for preventive healthcare, health promotion, and holistic patient management. Relevant literature published between 2018 and 2026 was identified through major electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, Embase, PsycINFO, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that AI improves healthcare accessibility, strengthens continuity of care, enhances diagnostic accuracy, supports personalized nursing interventions, and optimizes resource utilization. However, successful implementation requires addressing challenges related to ethical governance, algorithmic bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, interoperability, digital infrastructure, and AI competency among nurses. The review concludes that AI should function as a clinical decision-support tool that complements, rather than replaces, professional nursing judgment. Strategic investment in digital health education, interdisciplinary collaboration, and responsible AI governance will be essential for developing future-ready nurses capable of delivering equitable, evidence-based, and compassionate healthcare across diverse populations.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of distributed computer networks, driven by cloud computing, IoT ecosystems, edge computing, and software-defined infrastructures, has increased cybersecurity complexity. The growing volume, velocity, and variety of network data challenge traditional security mechanisms that focus primarily on threat detection, often neglecting system resilience, adaptive response, and recovery. This study develops a resilience-oriented intelligent big data analytics framework integrating Artificial Intelegence (AI), big data processing, and distributed cybersecurity monitoring to strengthen resilience in modern digital environments. A qualitative approach was employed through systematic literature review, conceptual modeling, thematic synthesis, and comparative analysis of existing architectures. The framework consists of four interconnected layers: data acquisition and aggregation, big data processing, intelligent analytics, and adaptive response and recovery. It supports continuous monitoring, anomaly detection, threat prediction, automated mitigation, and recovery orchestration. Comparative analysis indicates that prior studies focus mainly on improving intrusion detection or machine learning techniques, providing limited attention to resilience dimensions such as adaptability, fault tolerance, recovery efficiency, and operational stability. In contrast, the proposed framework integrates intelligent analytics with scalable big data infrastructures and distributed security mechanisms to create a unified resilience-oriented cybersecurity ecosystem. Findings suggest that combining AI-driven analytics, distributed processing, and adaptive security orchestration provides a strategic foundation for enhancing cybersecurity resilience, supporting sustainable digital infrastructure development, and ensuring operational stability in increasingly complex and interconnected network environments.

AbstractThe literature on Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management is dominated byGlobal-North evidence, while African evidence remains fragmented across country casestudies, public-sector surveys, and philosophical critiques. This systematic literaturereview consolidates 2020–2026 scholarship on AI-HRM in 32 African countries, applyingthe PRISMA 2020 framework and synthesizing evidence within a four-stage maturitymodel: Awareness, Experimentation, Operationalization, and Institutionalization. Across63 included studies, six cross-stage patterns emerge: AI is reshaping recruitment andselection efficiency; performance management is adopting AI tools unevenly acrosssectors; HR analytics maturity is highest in multinational subsidiaries; ethical riskconcentrates at the Institutionalization stage; Ubuntu and Afrocentric ethics are emergingas governance frameworks; and African-specific barriers include broadband penetration,fragmented AI policy, and low AI literacy among HR practitioners. The review contributesa stage-based diagnostic instrument, identifies boundary conditions for each stage, andsignals an Afrocentric research agenda for the next decade. Implications for HRpractitioners, organizational leaders, and African policy-makers are articulatedKeywordsArtificial Intelligence in HRM; Four-Stage Maturity Model, Ubuntu Philosophy;Afrocentric Ethics, Strategic Human Resource Management
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Culinary spices represent one of the most commonly adulterated agricultural commodities worldwide due to the complexity of their supply chain and the high economic value of the product. Traditional laboratory analyses (e.g., High-performance liquid chromatography, Mass spectrometry, and Wet chemical tests) are destructive, time-consuming, and insufficient for the high-throughput screening of spice powders or botanicals. This paper conducts a narrative literature review of 22 selected sources published between 2016 and 2026 that fall under seven themes: spice supply-chain risks and adulteration profiles, computer vision and deep learning approaches, portable Vis–NIR spectroscopy, electronic nose and gas sensing, multi-sensor fusion and chemometric analysis, machine learning methods for quantifying adulteration concentrations, and Edge-IoT hardware solutions. The reviewed articles demonstrate that Convolutional Neural Networks and transfer learning can reach an excellent level of precision in distinguishing between whole spices and botanical intruders, while compact Vis-NIR spectral sensors can detect food dyes and starch fillers in ground powders. SVM/Random Forest classifier-based MOS gas-sensor arrays can detect spoiled spices and vision-spectral fusion can have more accurate detection than a single modality. Nevertheless, most of the data presented in the literature is based on experiments performed on an oversimplified scenario of adulteration, and there are not enough publicly available multi-modal sensor datasets. This research presents a thematic literature review, a comparison of features in fourteen selected papers, a proposed conceptual framework, and recommendations.

This article offers a theoretical and methodological reflection on the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) and school leadership, on the assumption that the spread of intelligent systems constitutes an epistemological transformation capable of redefining educational governance, decision-making processes and school organisation. In line with the paradigm of complexity (Morin, 2001), innovation is not interpreted as the mere introduction of digital tools, but as a redefinition of the categories through which schools observe, interpret and govern the educational reality. AI therefore represents a pedagogical challenge even before it is a technological one, requiring leadership capable of integrating organisational, ethical, pedagogical and technological dimensions, and orienting them towards equity, participation and inclusion (Fullan, 2014). From this perspective, education continues to be aimed at human development (Biesta, 2022) and the expansion of people's capabilities (Nussbaum, 2011). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 307-310. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.

Humans have keen interests with artificial objects. We consume food and drinks containing artificial coloring while FIFA approves the use of artificial turf for football matches. However, the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has gripped the world with its radical changes, triggering not only physical, but also philosophical implications. In this paper, we explore the impact of AI on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and pose the question of whether the human centrality of the SDGs could diminish with the introduction of AI. Drawing on Kant’s concept of universalism and categorical imperatives, we argue that AI cannot safeguard intergenerational justice or meet Kant’s definition of a rational being. This paper presents a brief yet significant perspective, emphasizing the need for caution when integrating AI into the implementation of the SDGs, particularly concerning policy design.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) as a supportive agent in professional terminology work, using the Estonian national defence terminology as a case study. The study addresses the growing need to manage large volumes of multilingual defence-related documentation while simultaneously preserving expert-driven, concept-oriented terminology development practices. We present and evaluate a retrieval-augmented, large language model (LLM)-based prototype designed to extract and structure source-grounded (English) terminological raw material — such as definition candidates, related terms, usage contexts, and exact references — rather than to generate dictionary-ready entries. The prototype was evaluated through an expert-based assessment involving both domain specialists and experienced terminologists. The evaluation focused on the practical usefulness, contextual adequacy, and completeness of the extracted information, rather than on formal definitional correctness alone. The results indicate that the prototype performs reliably in retrieving definition candidates, contextual evidence, and source references, and can meaningfully support the early stages of terminology work. At the same time, persistent limitations were identified, including occasional hallucinations under weak source constraints, inconsistent handling of semantic relations, and challenges at the boundary between general and specialised language. The findings underscore the continued centrality of human expertise in terminology development and support a human-at-the-core model — as distinct from a human-in-the-loop model, where humans primarily correct machine output — in which AI functions as an assistive, context-sensitive tool rather than an autonomous terminological agent. The study contributes contextualised empirical evidence to ongoing debates on AI-assisted terminology management and offers methodological insights into prompt design, expert evaluation, and the integration of AI tools into institutional terminology workflows, particularly in small-language and national defence contexts.

This study evaluated four widely used large language models—ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek—as patient-information tools for e-Nabız, the national personal health record system of Türkiye, and tested whether their answers were reproducible one week apart. Thirty authentic patient questions spanning seven e-Nabız domains were submitted to each model in Turkish and English, in fresh sessions with default settings, and the protocol was repeated after one week (480 responses). A dated copy of the official e-Nabız User Guide served as the gold standard, and responses were scored blind for accuracy, completeness, the Global Quality Score, coverage, and safety, with readability computed using the Flesch, Flesch–Kincaid, Ateşman, and Bezirci–Yılmaz formulas. Model performance differed significantly in both languages, with Claude and Gemini outperforming ChatGPT and DeepSeek; two models performed better in Turkish. All models wrote above recommended reading levels, and although aggregate quality was stable between rounds, individual answers were substantially reworded and sometimes materially changed. Chatbots should complement, not replace, official e-Nabız guidance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping the operations, services, and user engagement strategies of modern libraries, including those in higher education and public domains. AI technologies, encompassing machine learning, natural language processing, chatbots, and predictive analytics, enable libraries to automate routine tasks, personalize information services, and generate data-driven insights for collection development and resource management. This paper examines the role of AI in modern libraries, focusing on three core dimensions: automation of cataloguing, classification, and reference services; intelligent discovery and personalized recommendation systems; and AI-driven analytics for decision-making and user engagement. The paper reviews the conceptual architecture of AI-enabled library systems, surveys current applications, and discusses the institutional, ethical, and technical challenges associated with adoption. It concludes by outlining future directions, including the convergence ofAI withIoTand cloud computing, forbuilding intelligent, adaptive library ecosystems.

The acceleration of the regulatory requirement, globalization of operations and digital transformation has increased the corporate vulnerability to legal risk. The current legal risk management methods which are mostly reactive and manual fail to handle the scale and complexity of the modern legal and compliance issues. Corporations are in turn moving towards artificial intelligence (AI) more and more as a method of improving legal risk identification, evaluation, and reduction. The paper explores the ways of using AI to balance the control of corporate legal risk and governance, accountability, and ethical responsibility. Using a qualitative and conceptual research of the existing literature, the study examines the major types of corporate legal risk such as regulatory compliance, contractual risk, litigation exposure, governance failures, and data protection issues. The paper examines AI applications within the corporate legal functions, including natural language processing, machine learning, and predictive analytics, and puts into the limelight, how these applications can be used to facilitate proactive and predictive risk management. Meanwhile, the paper critically considers the issues related to the use of AI such as algorithmic bias, transparency, threats to privacy, and legal accountability ambiguity. To resolve the challenges a conceptual framework is suggested, which incorporates the AI capabilities in the corporate level of legal risk management in a regulation-focused and ethically sound framework. The article adds to the literature because it offers a comprehensive view of AI-sensitive law risk management and offers useful data that corporations should consider in terms of finding the balance between innovation and legal accountability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) research in endodontics has grown quickly, but the strength of the evidence differs between applications. This narrative review with structured evidence mapping examined diagnostic imaging, canal morphology, outcome prediction, large language models (LLMs), robotics and augmented reality, and operational uses such as case-difficulty assessment, triage and scheduling. Methods: Two anchor reviews were combined with a documented PubMed search to 30 September 2026, and studies were classified by design, sample, reference standard, validation, and evidence of clinical utility. Results: Periapical lesion detection has the largest evidence base: one meta-analysis reported pooled sensitivity of 0.925 and specificity of 0.852, although most included studies were at risk of bias and none was prospective. Fracture detection relies mainly on ex vivo data and is sensitive to image resolution. Outcome models showed modest to moderate discrimination in single-centre data. LLM studies reported 40% to 100% correct, appropriate, or concordant responses across different benchmarks and scoring rules, and outputs varied on repeated querying. Difficulty-assessment and scheduling tools have appeared since 2020 but have not been evaluated prospectively in clinical workflow. Conclusions: Technical performance has not yet been shown to translate into clinical benefit, and AI in endodontics should currently be used only as clinician-supervised decision support.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare presents significant legal challenges concerning patient safety, data protection, and medical accountability. This study examines the adequacy of Indonesia's constitutional and statutory frameworks in protecting patients receiving AI-assisted healthcare services and identifies regulatory measures necessary to strengthen legal certainty. Employing a normative juridical approach, the research analyzes Article 28H(1) of the 1945 Constitution, Law No. 17 of 2023 concerning Health, and Law No. 27 of 2022 concerning Personal Data Protection through statutory, conceptual, and doctrinal legal analysis. The findings demonstrate that existing regulations provide a substantive foundation for patient rights, informed consent, professional responsibility, and medical data confidentiality. However, significant regulatory limitations remain regarding algorithmic transparency, clinical validation, continuous performance monitoring, human oversight, and the allocation of liability among healthcare professionals, institutions, and technology providers. The study argues that these limitations reflect insufficient operational specificity rather than a complete legal vacuum. Accordingly, it proposes an integrated, risk-based regulatory framework incorporating AI-specific clinical safeguards, transparent decision-making, strengthened data governance, and clearly defined accountability mechanisms. This research contributes to the development of Indonesian healthcare law by demonstrating how existing constitutional guarantees and statutory obligations can be operationalized to ensure patient protection while supporting responsible AI innovation.

documents.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in innovation activities, yet firm-level evidence on variation across innovation stages and organizational conditions remains limited in emerging economies such as Kazakhstan. This study examines AI use among surveyed firms in Kazakhstan, focusing on stage-specific influence, organizational correlates, barriers, reported effects, and managerial perceptions. A cross-sectional voluntary survey yielded a non-probability sample of 93 firms; data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests, exploratory bivariate analysis, multinomial logistic regression, and descriptive review of open-ended recommendations. In the sample, 39.8% reported no AI use in innovation activities; 23.7% used AI frequently or always. Idea generation was rated higher than idea testing and selection (r = .398), although concordance in stage rankings was weak (Kendall’s W = .077). The reported AI-related resource-category count was associated with both occasional (RRR = 6.98) and frequent AI use (RRR = 7.10) relative to no reported AI use in innovation activities. At the same time, firm size and age were not significant. Skills shortages, financial constraints, regulatory uncertainty, and ethical concerns were the leading barriers. Among firms reporting AI use in innovation activities, the most frequently reported effects were greater innovation-process efficiency (46.4%) and improved understanding of industry opportunities and trends (30.4%). The findings provide exploratory firm-level evidence and highlight the relevance of organizational resource support, pilot-based implementation, and human oversight.AcknowledgmentThis research was funded by the Science Committee of the Ministry of Science and Higher Education of the Republic of Kazakhstan (Grant No. AP23487651).The authors sincerely thank JSC "Center for International Programs" and the "500 Scientists" research internship program of the Republic of Kazakhstan. A. Zhidebekkyzy's participation in the "500 Scientists" program provided a valuable academic environment that inspired the initial idea for this study.

documents.abstract: This paper explores the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in legal research and judicial decision support. It examines the key technologies currently in use, the tangible benefits they offer (such as efficiency, cost reduction, and improved access to justice), and the critical risks that have emerged in practice (including algorithmic bias, opacity, automation bias, and confidentiality concerns). Furthermore, the paper proposes institutional governance measures and responsible workflows to ensure that AI innovation remains aligned with the core principles of the rule of law, including competence, candor, fairness, and reasoned decision-making. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Legal Tech, Judicial Decision Support, AI Ethics, Algorithmic Bias, Legal Research, AI Governance, Open Access
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most influential technologies shaping modern marketing. The rapid growth of digital platforms, customer data, and automated technologies has changed how businesses understand consumers, communicate with audiences, and measure marketing performance. AI enables organizations to analyse large datasets, predict consumer behaviour, personalize communication, automate routine tasks, and generate content. This research paper examines the role of AI in marketing, its major applications, benefits, challenges, ethical concerns, and future implications. The paper argues that AI can significantly improve marketing effectiveness when combined with human creativity, strategic judgment, and responsible data practices. At the same time, concerns regarding privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, transparency, and employment demonstrate the need for careful and ethical implementation. The future of marketing is therefore likely to depend on a collaborative relationship between human marketers and intelligent technologies.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most influential technologies shaping software engineering in recent years. This transformation has moved beyond early code generation and completion tools toward systems capable of participating in requirements analysis, design, testing, debugging, documentation, and solving complex software problems. The aim of this review paper is to examine the evolving role of AI in software engineering, with a particular focus on the transition from code generation tools to reasoning-based infrastructures. In this study, relevant research and studies on the application of Large Language Models (LLMs), code generation tools, and intelligent systems across different phases of the software development lifecycle are reviewed and categorized. The distinction between automatic code generation and capabilities such as problem analysis, planning, multi-step reasoning, and solution evaluation is also discussed. Findings from the reviewed literature indicate that AI can evolve from an auxiliary tool for generating code fragments into an effective factor in supporting more complex software engineering processes. However, issues such as output correctness, reasoning errors, code security, dependence on training data, trustworthiness, and the necessity of human oversight remain significant challenges in this field. Finally, the paper emphasizes the need to move from a purely "code generation" perspective toward a more comprehensive approach based on human–AI collaboration in software engineering processes.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the environments in which religious questions are explored, and values are interpreted and transmitted across generations. Although existing scholarship addresses digital religion and the ethical and educational implications of AI, the mechanisms through which conversational AI may influence intergenerational religious communication within families require further conceptual examination. This article develops a Responsible Relational AI Mediation Model grounded in family pedagogy, religious socialization theory, digital religion studies, AI ethics, and Catholic personalist anthropology. This study employs an interdisciplinary conceptual approach based on critical literature analysis and synthesis, supplemented by selected international policy documents and Catholic Church teaching. The proposed model integrates three analytical dimensions: structural, identifying the persons, relationships, communities, and technologies involved in religious formation; processual, examining how AI-generated interpretations may influence perceived authority and intergenerational dialogue; and normative, establishing criteria for responsible technological mediation. It distinguishes between relationally integrated and non-integrated pathways of AI-mediated religious inquiry and recognizes generative AI as an educational tool, a mediator of interpretation, and a potential environment for ongoing religious learning. This article argues that the formative significance of AI depends on how its use is connected with critical discernment, interpersonal relationships, and religious community participation. The model offers a conceptual framework for future empirical research rather than establishing causal effects of AI on religious formation.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in nursing management through workforce modelling, quality surveillance, resource allocation and organisational decision support. However, artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management remains conceptually underdeveloped, particularly regarding governance, accountability and nursing-specific leadership responsibilities. Objective: To analyse and define artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management and develop a conceptual framework for future empirical research, competency development and responsible AI implementation. Design: A concept analysis using Walker and Avant’s eight-step methodology, supported by a structured search to identify conceptually relevant interdisciplinary literature. Setting: Peer-reviewed interdisciplinary literature and authoritative policy and professional guidance documents identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, Europe PMC, ProQuest Nursing & Allied Health Database and relevant authoritative sources, published between 2020 and 2025. Main outcome measures: Defining attributes, antecedents, consequences, model cases and empirical referents. Results: Twenty-four substantive sources were retained for conceptual analysis; methodological and theoretical foundations were used separately to guide analysis and support theoretical positioning. Artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management was conceptualised as a governance-specialised extension of nursing leadership comprising five interrelated attributes: strategic AI direction-setting, managerial AI literacy, ethical and regulatory oversight, organisational change leadership and workforce capability development, and systematic integration into nursing management processes. Antecedents were organised as core or contextual conditions; consequences were differentiated into proximal and proposed distal consequences, the latter requiring empirical validation. Empirical referents were identified at individual, workforce and organisational levels. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence leadership in nursing management clarifies the leadership responsibilities required when AI informs nursing managerial decision-making, including algorithmic accountability, human oversight and preservation of professional nursing judgement. The concept provides a foundation for competency development, empirical validation and organisational governance across health and aged care settings, including Asia-Pacific contexts.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports financial decision-making, risk assessment, service innovation, and customer interaction. This study maps the Web of Science (WoS) -indexed literature on AI technologies in financial services and financial technology (FinTech) through a PRISMA-guided bibliometric analysis of 512 English-language articles published from 2016 to 2025. Performance analysis, VOSviewer co-word mapping, CiteSpace timeline analysis, and keyword burst detection are combined to examine publication patterns, research contributors, thematic structure, and changes in scholarly attention. The selected corpus shows rapid publication growth and three prominent co-word domains: AI-driven FinTech innovation, machine learning for credit risk and fraud detection, and user adoption of digital financial services. Temporal mapping and the recent burst of the keyword 'trust' indicate increasing scholarly interest in governance-related and user-oriented concerns, alongside established technical applications. These trends also highlight the relevance of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations, particularly AI sustainability, financial inclusion, and responsible governance. Drawing on these observed patterns, the study advances a socio-technical interpretation in which trustworthy AI governance is proposed as a conceptual linkage among innovation, risk management, and user adoption. The framework is an interpretive synthesis, not an empirically validated causal model. Because the study uses a predefined WoS-only search without formal cross-database or search-strategy sensitivity testing, the findings apply to the selected corpus and should not be regarded as exhaustive of the global literature. The resulting research agenda emphasises responsible management of information resources in AI-enabled financial services.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed higher education by providing tools that support research and academic writing. This action research study examined changes in graduate students' research and academic writing outcomes following a structured six-week instructional intervention integrating Perplexity AI and Jenni AI. Seventeen graduate students participated in workshops on the effective and ethical use of both tools. Data were collected using pre- and post-intervention questionnaires and an analytical rubric evaluating students' research papers. The mean rubric score increased from 62.51 (SD = 9.80) to 86.47 (SD = 6.59) out of 100, t (16) = 8.26, p < .001, 95% CI [17.81, 30.10], Cohen's dz = 2.00. The overall questionnaire mean increased from 3.17 (SD = 0.56) to 4.42 (SD = 0.51) on a five-point Likert scale, t (16) = 7.99, p < .001, 95% CI [0.92, 1.59], Cohen's dz = 1.94. Participation in the structured AI-supported intervention was associated with substantial improvements in research-paper performance and self-reported research, writing, and AI-related outcomes. The findings also underscore the importance of ethical use, critical evaluation, and human oversight. Given the small single-group design, the results should be interpreted as evidence of pre–post change rather than proof of a causal effect attributable to either AI tool.

Objectives: The effective prevention and control of cervical cancer (CC) depend on high-quality screening. However, traditional cytology interpretation faces challenges such as strong subjectivity, significant inter-observer variability, and a shortage of cytopathologists in primary care settings. The distribution of high-quality medical resources in China is highly uneven between urban and rural areas. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cytology offers a new approach to enhance screening efficacy. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a deep learning-based AI-assisted cytology system in a multicenter clinical environment in China, comparing its utility as a standalone tool and in a collaborative model with cytopathologists. Materials and Methods: This was a multicenter, crossover study enrolling a total of 769 outpatient liquid-based cytology samples obtained from three participating hospitals. Using a crossover design, two junior-to-mid-level cytopathologists from primary hospitals performed independent diagnoses and AI-assisted diagnoses (following an AI preliminary screening combined with cytopathologist verification), which were compared with AI-alone diagnoses. Using an expert cytology panel diagnosis as the cytological reference standard, sensitivity (Se), specificity (Sp), overall accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV) negative predictive value, and false-positive rates/false-negative rates and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) were calculated and compared for each modality at the atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US+), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL+), and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL+) thresholds. Results: The study found that the independent diagnostic Se of the primary cytopathologists was insufficient (LSIL+: 46.0% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.359–0.564)–50.6% (95% CI: 0.403–0.608); HSIL+: 36.6% (95% CI: 0.236–0.519)–46.3% (95% CI: 0.321–0.613), indicating a high risk of missed diagnoses. AI-alone diagnosis showed high Se (ASC-US+: 92.9% [95% CI: 0.877–0.960]) but a relatively lower PPV (72.0% [95% CI: 0.654–0.778]). AI-assisted diagnostic model achieved a favorable balance. Across all diagnostic thresholds, the AI-assisted modality significantly outperformed cytopathologist-alone diagnosis. At the ASC-US+ threshold, AI-alone Se was 92.9% (95% CI: 0.877–0.960) with a Sp of 90.9% (95% CI: 0.883–0.929), whereas the sensitivities of the two primary cytopathologists alone were 68.4% (95% CI: 0.607–0.752) and 81.3% (95% CI: 0.744–0.866), respectively. With AI assistance, primary cytopathologist Se increased to 92.3% (95% CI: 0.870–0.955)–94.2% (95% CI: 0.893–0.969), and Sp reached 94.6% (95% CI: 0.925–0.961)–96.9% (95% CI: 0.952–0.980). At the LSIL+ and HSIL+ thresholds, where cytopathologist-alone sensitivities were low (LSIL+: 46.0% [95% CI: 0.359–0.564]–50.6% [95% CI: 0.403–0.608]; HSIL+: 36.6% [95% CI: 0.236–0.519]–46.3% [95% CI: 0.321–0.613]), AI assistance improved them to 80.5% (95% CI: 0.709–0.874) and 73.2% (95% CI: 0.581–0.843)–75.6% (95% CI: 0.607–0.862), respectively, with Sp exceeding 97.0% in both cases. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis confirmed that the AUC for AI-assisted diagnosis (0.938 [95% CI: 0.911–0.965]–0.971 [95% CI: 0.946–0.996]) was significantly higher than that for cytopathologist-alone diagnosis (0.791 [95% CI: 0.746–0.836]–0.868 [95% CI: 0.819–0.918]). Conclusion: In this exploratory study, the AI-assisted cytology system may help reduce the experience gap for primary cytopathologists in primary hospitals, substantially improving the Se and Sp of cervical cytology interpretation. The AI-assisted diagnostic model is an effective strategy for achieving standardized, high-quality CC screening, particularly for promoting homogeneous services in regions with uneven healthcare resources.

documents.abstract: Abstract Equitable digital education is central to Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). Yet as digital systems shape how education is delivered, assessed and governed, a deeper divide is emerging between countries that can merely adopt educational technologies and those that can develop, adapt and govern them. This study examines the global distribution of technology-shaping capacity in education using 274,825 educational-technology patent records filed from 2006 to 2025. We combine four-period spatial mapping, concentration measures, 16 technology themes, annual trajectories, and LightGBM-SHAP interpretation of high-value patents from 2013 to 2023. Geographic participation expanded after 2011, yet inventive activity remained strongly concentrated: the leading country accounted for 63.48–77.62% of records across the three mature periods, while the five leading countries consistently exceeded 90%. Innovation shifted from stand-alone teaching tools toward virtual reality, artificial intelligence, adaptive learning, platform-based services and data-intensive systems. Geographic, technological and temporal variables contributed 33.33%, 27.03% and 25.78%, respectively, to the prediction of high-value patents, and high-value inventions were concentrated in a limited set of country-theme pathways. These patterns reveal a capability divide overlooked by connectivity indicators. Education systems may gain access to advanced tools without gaining the capacity to adapt them to local languages and curricula, audit algorithms, govern data or develop alternatives. By revealing where technology-shaping capacity and high-value innovation are concentrated, this study can help policymakers identify priorities for capability building, technology transfer and governance support to advance more inclusive and sustainable digital transformation toward SDG 4.

Abstract Objective:Accurate interpretation of planar ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy, used for diagnosing pulmonary embolism (PE) based on PIOPED/EANM guidelines, requires objective assessment of mismatched V/Q defects. Manual delineation of V/Q defects is time-consuming, subject to interobserver variability, and rarely performed in practice, limiting standardized reporting and quantification of disease burden. To address these challenges, we evaluated four modern AI models for automated segmentation of vascular perfusion defects in planar V/Q scans and compared their performance to human annotators.Approach:We retrospectively identified 2,118 patients who underwent planar V/Q scans at The Ottawa Hospital (June 2019-February 2023). Six standard projections (ANT, POST, LAO, RAO, LPO, RPO) were included. Four 2D neural networks (U-Net, nnU-Net, Swin UNETR, and a Bottleneck Transformer U-Net [BTU-Net]) were trained on 1,313 patients (7,878 projections) and validated on 329 (1,974 projections) using physician-annotated defects. A hold-out test set of 46 high probability patients was used to evaluate segmentation quality, and defect detection accuracy using free-response receiver operating characteristic (FROC) analysis.Main results:BTU-Net was the only model performing on par with human readers, showing robust sensitivity across the entire range of segmentation probabilities. At 1.5 false positives per projection rate (FPPR), BTU-Net outperformed other models with sensitivity of 0.529 ± 0.026, On a separate hold-out set of low likelihood of disease patients (n=430), the lowest FPPR was 0.08 ± 0.01 for BTU-Net (P<0.0001).Significance:BTU-Net enables rapid, consistent, and accurate interpretation of planar V/Q scans. Such tools may enhance diagnostic efficiency, standardize reporting, and support non-expert readers in evaluating PE.

documents.abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains the cornerstone of revascularization in coronary artery disease. However, despite advances in stent technology, adverse outcomes related to suboptimal stent placement including under-expansion, malapposition, incomplete coverage, edge dissection, and neoatherosclerosis persist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the highest resolution widely available intravascular imaging modality, allowing unparalleled visualization of stent-vessel interactions and plaque morphology. However, there are significant barriers to large-scale OCT adoption, including time-consuming manual interpretation and dependence on the operator, resulting in significant variability between analysts. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated OCT analysis promises to assist PCI by delivering rapid, reproducible, and standardized stent optimization, but current analysis systems lack important features to optimize stent placement. This review summarizes the principles of OCT in PCI, the evidence for OCT-guided optimization, and recent advances in AI-driven automated OCT analysis. We discuss plaque analysis and classification, highlighting how AI-driven automated OCT analysis can identify fibrous, lipid-rich, and calcified lesions and guide tailored lesion preparation using balloons, specialty balloons, drug-coated balloons, intravascular lithotripsy, and atherectomy. We outline emerging AI-enabled workflows for fully automated PCI optimization, evaluate clinical outcomes, interpretability, and workflow integration. Finally, we explore future directions including AI imaging-physiology fusion, multiomics integration, and robotics. If successful, automated AI-empowered OCT analysis could become a central imaging platform for precision PCI, enabling tailored lesion preparation, optimal stent deployment, and improved clinical outcomes in coronary artery disease management.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract: Health-related social needs such as housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers are associated with worse health outcomes and increased health care utilization, particularly among older adults. Although health systems increasingly screen for these needs, many lack the capacity to provide follow-up support at scale. This pilot evaluation described the implementation and early operational performance of an artificial intelligence-supported, on-demand patient navigation service integrated into an urban safety-net health system. From July 2024 to March 2025, providers placed 149 referrals from family medicine and geriatrics clinics. Outreach was attempted for all referred patients, and successful contact occurred for 78 patients. Navigators submitted 301 applications for public benefits and community resources; 145 were approved, while others remained pending or in process at analysis. Program costs during the observation period were approximately $5,000. These findings suggest feasibility while highlighting the need for further evaluation of patient experience and outcomes.
topics: Food Security and Health in Diverse Populations

documents.abstract: Attention to students' emotional dimension represents a key determinant of both academic success and future personal and social development (Weber et al., 2016). Within this perspective, the design of emotionally meaningful learning experiences, including those supported by Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based conversational technologies, can enhance students' well-being and engagement by recognizing emotions as a fundamental component of learning processes. Through Natural Language Processing techniques and affective computing models, intelligent conversational systems can detect and interpret users' emotional states and dynamically adapt interactions accordingly. In particular, so-called empathic conversational agents (Ortega-Ochoa et al., 2024) are artificial entities designed to elicit empathic responses from users (Hall & Woods, 2006) and to generate highly personalized simulated environments by modulating content, feedback, and task difficulty according to identified emotional factors. Such artificial conversations enable learners to engage in adaptive learning experiences in which their emotional state becomes an active variable in the regulation of the educational pathway. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 116-117. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers scalable feedback on student writing; however, its effects on writing performance and motivation relative to teacher feedback remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on Feedback Intervention Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this study examined the comparative effectiveness of AI-generated and teacher-provided feedback on students’ writing performance and motivational outcomes. Methods A randomized controlled study assigned 312 undergraduate students to one of three conditions: AI-generated feedback, teacher feedback, or a control condition without substantive feedback. A total of 287 participants were included in the analyses. The study evaluated revised-essay quality, feedback engagement, writing self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, perceived relatedness to the feedback source, and AI literacy. Results Both AI-generated feedback and teacher feedback produced higher revised-essay quality than the control condition, with effect sizes of d = 0.60 and d = 0.59, respectively. The two feedback conditions were statistically equivalent within a prespecified equivalence margin of ±0.35 standard deviations. Feedback engagement, but not writing self-efficacy, statistically accounted for the observed performance advantage. Teacher feedback elicited higher intrinsic motivation than AI-generated feedback, although AI-generated feedback also yielded higher intrinsic motivation than the control condition. This motivational difference was associated with perceived relatedness to the feedback source. The indirect effects identified in the analyses are associational rather than causal. AI literacy did not significantly moderate the effect of feedback on writing performance ( p = 0.058). Discussion Within the context of a single feedback-and-revision cycle at one institution, the findings suggest that AI-generated feedback can achieve writing-performance outcomes comparable to those of teacher feedback, while providing weaker motivational support. These results highlight the potential value of blended feedback approaches that combine the scalability of AI-generated feedback with the relational and motivational strengths of teacher–student interaction. Further research across multiple institutions and repeated feedback cycles is needed to establish the generalizability and longer-term implications of these findings.

The integration of artificial intelligence is generating rapid transformations in society and, particularly, in higher education institutions. Its incorporation offers significant opportunities for teaching and learning processes, but it also raises challenges related to academic integrity, privacy, bias, authorship, equity, plagiarism, and the generation of false information. This reflective essay aims to analyze the main ethical aspects associated with the use of artificial intelligence in higher education institutions and to highlight the responsibilities of the different actors within the educational community. Methodologically, the study adopted a qualitative, documentary, and reflective approach based on the critical analysis of recent scientific literature and documents from international organizations addressing ethics and the use of artificial intelligence in educational contexts. The analysis highlights the need to establish clear institutional policies, regulations, and guidelines that promote the ethical, transparent, and responsible use of these technologies. It is concluded that higher education institutions play a fundamental role in regulating their use, educating students and faculty, and promoting continuous ethical reflection to ensure that technological innovation is aligned with academic integrity, the protection of rights, and human responsibility.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: RESUMO O assédio moral constitui forma de violência psicológica capaz de degradar o ambiente de trabalho, comprometer a saúde do trabalhador e afetar a eficiência institucional. Nas Polícias Militares e nos Corpos de Bombeiros Militares estaduais, a análise do fenômeno exige especial cautela, porque o exercício legítimo da autoridade convive com estruturas rígidas de hierarquia e disciplina. Este artigo examina os elementos caracterizadores do assédio moral, suas formas de manifestação e suas consequências, distinguindo-o do poder regular de comando, fiscalização e correção. Adota-se pesquisa qualitativa, bibliográfica e documental, com análise da Constituição Federal, da Lei nº 6.880/1980, da Lei nº 14.751/2023, do Código Penal Militar, de proposições legislativas e de literatura especializada. Sustenta-se que hierarquia e disciplina não autorizam humilhação, perseguição, discriminação ou desvio de finalidade. Embora ainda não exista tipo penal federal específico e vigente de assédio moral no Código Penal Militar, o fato pode produzir responsabilização civil, administrativa e, conforme as circunstâncias, penal. Conclui-se que a prevenção depende de liderança ética, canais protegidos de denúncia, apuração imparcial, proteção contra retaliações, formação continuada e acompanhamento da saúde ocupacional, sem enfraquecimento dos fundamentos constitucionais das instituições militares. Palavras-chave: assédio moral; militares estaduais; hierarquia; disciplina; abuso de poder; saúde ocupacional. ABSTRACT Workplace bullying is a form of psychological violence capable of degrading the work environment, harming workers' health and impairing institutional effectiveness. In State Military Police and State Military Fire Brigades, its assessment requires particular caution because legitimate authority operates within rigid structures of hierarchy and discipline. This article examines the defining elements, manifestations and consequences of workplace bullying, distinguishing it from lawful command, supervision and correction. It adopts a qualitative, bibliographic and documentary approach based on the Federal Constitution, Federal Laws No. 6,880/1980 and No. 14,751/2023, the Military Criminal Code, legislative proposals and specialized literature. The study argues that hierarchy and discipline do not authorize humiliation, persecution, discrimination or misuse of authority. Although no specific and effective federal criminal offense of workplace bullying currently exists in the Military Criminal Code, abusive conduct may result in civil, administrative and, depending on the circumstances, criminal liability. Prevention requires ethical leadership, protected reporting channels, impartial investigations, safeguards against retaliation, continuing education and occupational health monitoring, without weakening the constitutional foundations of military institutions. Keywords: workplace bullying; state military personnel; hierarchy; discipline; abuse of authority; occupational health.

Objective. Assess occupational health and safety (OHS) workforce needs across Public Health Region 6 (PHR 6)—Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas—to identify gaps, priorities, and capacity-building opportunities and to inform national OHS priorities. Methods. A mixed-methods needs assessment integrated stakeholder engagement, national OHS professional and alumni surveys, federal dataset analysis, Education and Research Center (ERC) program records, literature review, and job market surveillance. Results. Demand for OHS professionals is projected to grow, particularly for safety specialists and industrial hygienists. Key unmet needs include mental health, workplace violence prevention, and exposure assessment. PHR 6 also experiences high occupational fatality rates and climate-related environmental burdens. Conclusions. Sustained investment in workforce development, interdisciplinary training, and outreach is essential to advance worker health equity and inform national OHS priorities.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This article argues that AI-governed systems, and large language models in particular, introduce a novel dynamic into contemporary figurations: one of asymmetric dependency, in which people are materially, and increasingly affectively, dependent upon systems that are not, in turn, affectively dependent upon them. This condition attenuates the affectively reciprocal interdependency on which psychogenetic processes depend in Norbert Elias’s account of the civilising process and gives rise to what we distinguish as behavioural civilising: the shaping of observable conduct through monitored compliance rather than through the internalisation of restraint. Because such systems simulate human exchange whilst stripping it of its negative social consequences, they simultaneously suspend the shame functions through which figurational pressure is ordinarily converted into self-restraint and so exert decivilising pressures within the same figuration. Extended engagement with conversational AI also introduces generative reflection: a mode of exchange in which thought is elaborated and transformed rather than merely returned. We thereby extend the Eliasian framework whilst specifying the conditions under which psychogenetic processes are disrupted and transformed.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational contexts is profoundly transforming teaching and learning processes, creating new opportunities for personalized instruction while simultaneously raising pedagogical, ethical, and professional challenges (Chen et al., 2020; ZawackiRichter et al., 2019). While traditional technology acceptance models have primarily emphasized the role of digital competencies and perceived usefulness (Davis, 1989; Venkatesh et al., 2003), more recent studies suggest that AI adoption is also shaped by emotional factors, including anxiety, distrust, fears of professional replacement, and concerns about the quality of the educational relationship (Schepman & Rodway, 2020; Liu & Liu, 2025). Within this framework, the present study investigates the combined contribution of cognitive and emotional factors to the development of attitudes toward Artificial Intelligence, assuming that AI acceptance is a multidimensional process in which knowledge, competencies, and emotional experiences interact dynamically.
